headline: I build the layer
underneath
feature teams.
hero.lede: Frontend platform engineer at GoDaddy. My users are other engineers.

machine.heading: Every release used to be walked across four repositories by hand.
machine.sub: So I built the thing that walks it. Press play.

outcomes.title: Deploys stopped batching
outcomes.body: Teams had been deferring releases rather than hand-trace package ownership. Removing the handoff removed the reason to wait.

outcomes.title: A defect class closed
outcomes.body: Shared-package versions used to ship decoupled from the changes they belonged to. Reconciliation makes that state unrepresentable.

outcomes.title: The merge stayed human
outcomes.body: Deliberately. The system generates a validated draft PR and stops.

metrics.label: automated bumps merged in early adoption

projects.title: A central release-orchestration layer
projects.body: Producer repo emits standard release metadata, a central layer validates it, and the downstream repo or deployment path picks it up. Repeated release logic lives behind reusable workflows and composite actions instead of being copy-pasted into every repository. Existing pipelines plug into it rather than being rewritten.

projects.title: Merge queues that actually validate
projects.body: A merge queue evaluates a temporary merge-group state, not the PR head — so required checks have to understand that path or they are validating the wrong thing. I made merge-group validation correct first, then cut waste: selective execution, cancelling superseded runs, and reusing cached build output.

projects.title: One component, many brands
projects.body: Theme and intent abstractions that separate behavior and semantics from brand presentation, so shared React infrastructure serves several brand experiences without forking a component per brand.

projects.title: Sticky-stack: independent roots, one stack
projects.body: The CMS could render three sticky navigation elements as separate React roots, so top: 0 made them collide — no shared parent owned the layout. I built a portal-based stacking surface with a registry, deterministic ordering and measured dynamic offsets, exposed to product teams as a single hook.

projects.title: CMS to components, server-side
projects.body: I contributed to the CMS modernization on the shared rendering layer: content transforms, a facade and component map, and shared packages that behave the same on the server as in the browser — no assumed window, no hydration surprises.

projects.title: A React bootcamp I wrote and taught
projects.body: Four hours, a progressive repository with structured branches, exercises and live instruction for interns. Turning what I know into something the team keeps is the same instinct as building a platform, just aimed at people.

about.heading: I kept drifting toward the layer underneath
about.sub: I started in product-facing React work, but the things I kept volunteering for were one layer down. The word for what I'm after is leverage: a feature ships once, a platform gets used for years.
more: That thread runs through all of it — shared component architecture, theme and intent APIs, sticky-stack, release orchestration, merge queues, the bootcamp I wrote for interns.

I'm also careful about what I claim. If I tell you a system saved time, I'll tell you how I'd measure it — and where I haven't yet. That habit has made me better at platform work than any framework has.
